events.excerpt: Posting a factual decode of recent ACLManager role activity on Aave V3 Ethereum, in the dated-report style already used in this category. Three RISK_ADMIN_ROLE grants since 2 September 2026: 2 Sep 2026, block 25891729 — granted to 0xbe28…7744 and 0x529e…F6c5 (two grants, same transaction) 30 Sep 2026, block 26089561 — granted to 0x6f48d9cdb8ee6e17c96b2d8aec128af426a295c1 The 30 Sep recipient is a verified contract named RiskSteward, 20,061 bytes of deployed code. All three grants were sent by 0x5300A1a15135EA4dc7aD5a167152C01EFc9b192A, which is the governance Executor. So these passed governance rather than originating from a standalone admin key — worth stating explicitly, since a RISK_ADMIN grant from an EOA would read very differently. Practical scope: RISK_ADMIN can change supply and borrow caps, LTVs, liquidation thresholds and reserve configuration without a full governance vote. Routing it through a RiskSteward contract constrains what the holder may change, which is the safer pattern, but each grant still widens the set of actors who can move risk parameters between votes. Context: the ARFC “Activate Aave Risk Stewards on Aave V4” thread is now closed with AIP #523 executed, so I’m posting this separately rather than reverting that thread. Method note: this is decoded from ACLManager’s RoleGranted logs plus the role constants read off the contract itself. events.excerpt: Last week’s security notice on the Fearless Wallet browser extension ( notice ) says that from February 2025, unlocking the wallet sent your private key to a server run by the attacker. The notice links a write-up that walks through the code at fixed commits ( write-up ). I read it and then went through the repo history myself. None of it was hidden. It sat in public source the whole time. I audit smart contracts, not browser extensions, but the review lessons carry over to any code that touches keys. Like the write-up, I’m sticking to what the code and the history show, not who wrote it or why. How it got in, and how it left The code arrived in PR #1022 of soramitsu/fearless-wallet-web, titled “Ton Service”. It was open for ten weeks and merged on 19 February 2025 as one squashed commit, “TON ecosystem”: 251 files, 4,690 lines added and 6,119 removed. The PR has no review comments. The function that matters is about 25 lines, in a new 180 line file, inside a diff of almost 11,000 changed lines whose title says it adds TON. It left the same way. The code was deleted from the source on 25 June 2026, inside a release commit with about 80,000 changed lines. What each piece looked like in a diff The name. On every unlock the extension calls fetchJettonInfo() . Jettons are TON tokens, so in a TON PR that reads like a token info fetch. What it actually does is export the recovery phrase of every main account (or the keystore file plus the wallet password) and send it out. The password. The keyring service keeps the typed password in this.password at unlock. That’s what lets later

events.excerpt: India’s Computer Emergency Response Team has warned the nation’s financial services industry of a “significant escalation” in attacks by what it describes as an “AI-assisted financial threat actor” that has re-targeted victims after they flubbed remediation efforts. CERT-IN first detected the attacks in October and issued advisory in which it warned digital lending platforms, fintech entities, payment service providers, and wallet operators that attackers were targeting internet-facing applications, exposed APIs and privileged endpoints. If the attackers found a way in, they tried to use payment APIs to steal money. On Thursday, the CERT published an update in which it said it continues to hear of successful attacks, including from outfits that tried to remediate their systems after earlier incidents. “The same entities have been deliberately re-targeted, including after incomplete remediation and attacks have been timed to coincide with holidays, weekends and other low-monitoring windows to delay detection and response,” the CERT warned. CERT-IN has decided the attackers need a name and chose “CRAFTY FALCON.” The security org has also revealed that the crew uses AI-enhanced tools including the ARTEX pen-testing tool, the Cairn attack search engine, and the CyberStrikeAI framework – all of which have been linked to users who appear to speak Chinese . CRAFTY FALCON’s tactics see it go looking for internet-exposed environments used for testing or development, where it finds artefacts such as shared credentials, tokens, or network paths that help it move into production system
events.title: Threat actor targets Indian fintechs on weekends when defenders aren’t watching

Dates are aims, not commitments. 1. Context Two complementary developments were proposed that could affect validators in the near future. The first is the move to Metanodes, described in a forum post by Adrian . Besides relay chain consensus, validators would take on node roles that the ecosystem currently funds separately, starting with collation and full nodes for Asset Hub and People Chain, potentially with further roles such as Bulletin Chain as opt-in. Over time, this could replace the separately funded RPC, collator and bootnode setups. For validators, it would mean more work per node and stronger hardware. The hardware requirements are published in the Polkadot docs. The second is a smaller active set.
